newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end little changed, profit-take seen.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end little changed, profit-take seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed little changed on Thursday after a profit-taking wave ahead of Friday's key employment report erased most of the market's early gains, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up a slight 1/32 at 98-28/32. Its yield was at 6.84 percent.

Experts said the selling spree was triggered by foreign investors who liquidated U.S. Treasuries positions after some European bond markets -- mainly Spain and Italy -- dropped after being higher earlier in the session.

"The Italian and Spanish bond markets began to collapse ... and that forced European accounts to start to dump Treasuries," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Yamaichi International (America) Inc.
At the opening of business in New York, Treasuries had rallied sharply on short-covering after some large Japanese accounts bought heavily in overnight trading.
"Some Japanese accounts bought strongly overnight, forcing New York to scramble to cover that short. London probably had to scramble to cover that as well," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Some analysts said rising oil prices also weighed on the U.S. government debt market and contributing to erase the day's early gains.
"Some people began to register some small concern over inflation. Why? Look at oil," Strauss said. "Look what's done the last month and what's done today and that fueled some of the selling as well."

In late afternoon trading, the November crude contract could not get above the $24.65 intra-day resistance. But the contract was up a sharp 52 cents in the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) at $24.57 a barrel.

On the other hand, analysts said the market took in some comments from St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank President Thomas Melzer and the head of the Richmond Fed Alfred Broaddus which confirmed the idea of a tame inflation scene.
"We did get favorable statements from Fed officials regarding the lack of inflation," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
On the economic indicator front, the market took in a bigger-than-expected drop in August factory orders, which were down 1.9 percent. That was the biggest drop since January 1993.
Jobless claims were at 340,000 in the September 28 week, unchanged from the prior seven-day period. "The data were actually good for the market," Thayer said.
The market is now gearing up for the key September employment report to be released on Friday. The indicator is expected to come in on the weak side.
In a Reuters poll, economists expect the non-farm payrolls to rise 166,000 in September against a 250,000 rise in August.
"We're anticipanting that we're going to see a weaker number than we've seen most of this year," Thayer said.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 4.90 percent. The six-month bill rate was up one basis point at 5.10 percent. The year bill rate was ucnhanged at 5.29 percent.

The two-year note closed off 1/32 at 100-0/32, yielding 6.00 percent. The five-year note traded down 1/32 at 100-4/32 to yield 6.35 percent. The ten-year note closed flat at 102-27/32, yielding 6.60 percent.
